title: SSAO: From View-Space Samples to an Occlusion Term
abstract: How a tangent-space hemisphere, projection, depth reconstruction, and range-weighted comparison produce screen-space ambient occlusion.
image: /content/blog/SSAO - From View-Space Samples to an Occlusion Term/ssao-sampling.svg
imageAlt: A view-space hemisphere projects sample points into a depth buffer where closer geometry contributes to ambient occlusion
lede: Screen-space ambient occlusion estimates how much nearby geometry hides the hemisphere above a visible surface. The shader never traces the complete scene. It builds candidate points around the current pixel in view space, projects each point back into the depth buffer, and asks whether the visible surface at that screen coordinate lies in front of the candidate.

sections.heading: What SSAO can observe
paragraphs: Ambient occlusion is a visibility term for indirect light. A point inside a corner sees less of the surrounding hemisphere than a point on an open plane, so its indirect contribution is reduced. SSAO approximates this relationship from the current camera's depth and normal buffers in a post-process pass.

That makes cost largely independent of scene polygon count, but it also defines the limitation: the depth buffer normally stores one visible surface per pixel. Geometry behind that layer, outside the viewport, or too thin to survive sampling is unavailable to the estimator.

equations.label: Conceptual ambient visibility
equations.expression: A(P) = 1 - (1 / pi) integral_over_hemisphere V(P, omega) W(omega) d omega

terms.text: Ambient visibility at surface point P; one is open and zero is fully occluded.

sections.heading: Put every comparison in view space
paragraphs: The center position, center normal, kernel sample, and sampled scene position must use the same coordinate system. View space is convenient because the camera is at the origin and depth follows a known view axis. This article assumes a DirectX-style positive-forward view space, so larger z values are farther from the camera.

A world-space position buffer can be transformed with the view matrix. A hardware depth value cannot: it is a non-linear projection result, not an xyz position. Reconstruct a view-space position with the inverse projection, or linearize depth with the exact projection parameters used to render it. Transform normals as vectors with w = 0, then normalize them.

callouts.title: Know what the G-buffer stores
callouts.text: If a texture stores world position, transform it as a point. If it stores device depth, reconstruct it through the inverse projection. Treating device depth as world xyz produces a plausible-looking but incorrect comparison.

sections.heading: Rotate a hemisphere around the surface normal
paragraphs: A reusable kernel stores random points inside a hemisphere whose local +z axis is its normal. For each pixel, construct a tangent-bitangent-normal basis that rotates this kernel onto the visible surface. A small tiled noise texture changes the tangent direction across pixels, trading structured banding for high-frequency noise that can be filtered later.

Project the random vector onto the plane perpendicular to the normal. The normalized result is the tangent; crossing the normal and tangent produces the bitangent. If the random vector is almost parallel to the normal, choose a fallback axis before normalizing so the basis does not become undefined.

sections.heading: Place and project each sample
paragraphs: Transform one kernel offset by the TBN matrix, scale it by the view-space radius, and add it to the center position. The result is a three-dimensional candidate point near the current surface.

The shader then projects that point to clip space, divides xy by w to obtain normalized device coordinates, and remaps NDC from [-1, 1] into texture UVs. The vertical sign in the remap depends on the graphics API and texture convention; the code below uses a top-left texture origin. Reject points behind the camera or outside the viewport.

equations.label: Homogeneous projection
equations.expression: clip = Projection * float4(sampleVS, 1); NDC.xy = clip.xy / clip.w; UV = NDC.xy * (0.5, -0.5) + 0.5

terms.text: Homogeneous scale introduced by projection; perspective division is required before the UV remap.

sections.heading: Compare the candidate with visible depth
paragraphs: Sample the depth buffer at the projected UV and reconstruct the visible scene depth in view space. Under the positive-forward convention, the scene occludes the candidate when the scene surface is closer to the camera than the candidate: sceneZ is less than sampleZ. A small bias prevents the center surface from occluding itself because of precision and interpolation error.

A range weight suppresses unrelated surfaces that happen to project onto the same UV but are far away in depth. An optional normal-direction weight can favor samples aligned with the surface hemisphere. Sum the weighted binary tests, divide by the valid weight or sample count, invert to ambient visibility, and apply a power only as an art-directed contrast control.

equations.label: Discrete SSAO estimate
equations.expression: visibility = pow(saturate(1 - sum(occluded_i * weight_i) / max(sum(weight_i), epsilon)), power)

terms.text: One when visible depth lies in front of candidate i, otherwise zero.
Range and optional direction weight for sample i.
Contrast control; it changes appearance, not visibility evidence.

callouts.title: The inequality is convention-dependent
callouts.text: Negative-forward view space, reverse-Z storage, and APIs with different clip conventions can reverse or otherwise change the test. Convert both values to one documented linear view-space convention before comparing them.

sections.heading: Noise is part of the sampling strategy
paragraphs: A small kernel cannot integrate every direction, so a fixed pattern creates visible bands. Rotating or jittering the pattern per pixel breaks those bands into noise. A depth- and normal-aware bilateral filter can then smooth samples from the same surface while preserving silhouettes and creases better than a plain box blur.

Temporal accumulation can reuse evidence across frames, but it needs motion vectors, rejection tests, and clamping to avoid trails. Half-resolution SSAO reduces texture work, although upsampling must again respect depth and normals to prevent halos.

rows: More depth reads and shader cost
technicalTables.caption: Tune radius in view or world units first; use power last because it only reshapes the output.

sections.heading: Read artifacts as missing information
paragraphs: A bright edge can mean that the occluder moved off-screen. A dark halo can mean that a large radius sampled a different depth layer. Flicker can mean that the sparse kernel changed coverage as geometry moved through pixels. These are not random defects; each one points to information the current depth image did not preserve or the filter mixed incorrectly.

SSAO is therefore most convincing as a local contact and crease term, not a replacement for complete indirect-light visibility. Keep its scale bounded, combine it with the engine's indirect-light model, and verify the result while the camera and objects move.
bullets: Use a linear view-space radius so the effect has a stable scene scale.
Reject or downweight large depth differences before they become halos.
Use edge-aware spatial or temporal filtering for sparse kernels.
Expect missing occlusion from off-screen and hidden geometry.
Debug center position, normal, projected UV, reconstructed depth, and the binary comparison as separate views.

closing: The SSAO loop is a sequence of coordinate-space contracts: reconstruct the visible surface in view space, rotate a local hemisphere around its normal, project each candidate back to the depth buffer, compare linear depths under one sign convention, and filter the sparse estimate without crossing real edges. Most SSAO bugs are one broken contract in that chain.
